note.title: Personal and reflexive pronouns
note.overview: Recall first- and second-person forms and the reflexive se sui sibi se pattern.
learningGoals: Recall first and second person pronoun forms.
Recall se sui sibi se in singular and plural.
mustMemoriseRules: The third-person reflexive has no nominative form.
se sui sibi se is the same in singular and plural.

workedExamples.prompt: TYPE THE ANSWER — Write the ablative form of first person plural we.

workedExamples.prompt: BUILD THE FORM — Write the accusative form of first person plural we.
workedExamples.why: The preferred school-sheet form is nos.

workedExamples.prompt: TYPE THE ANSWER — Write the accusative form of first person plural we.
workedExamples.why: The preferred school-sheet form is nos.

workedExamples.prompt: TYPE THE ANSWER — Write the dative form of first person plural we.
workedExamples.why: The preferred school-sheet form is nobis.

workedExamples.prompt: TYPE THE ANSWER — Write the genitive form of first person plural we.
workedExamples.why: The preferred school-sheet form is nostrum. Valid alternate accepted: nostri.

commonMistakes: Confusing mihi with mei or tibi with tui.
A familiar stem with the wrong case, number, person or tense ending is not correct.
detailedExplanation: Recall first- and second-person forms and the reflexive se sui sibi se pattern.

Latin noun endings show the word's grammatical job as well as number. Identify the dictionary form and stem, decide the required case and number from the sentence, then select the ending. Translate the function, not simply the first familiar meaning.
examTips: Mark the finite verb first, then use noun endings to assign subject, object and recipient roles.
Normal Latin word order can vary; the case, number, gender, person and tense endings cannot.
For English to Latin, build each required form before arranging the sentence.
